explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is not an end-user application but a large, modular client‐side JavaScript framework (AngularJS) designed to be embedded into web pages. Its purpose is to provide an MV* style architecture, two‐way data binding, dependency injection, templating and a full suite of core and optional modules (ngAnimate, ngRoute, ngResource, etc.) for building rich single-page applications.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - src/           ← Core framework code broken into subpackages:  
       • Angular.js, AngularPublic.js – bootstrapping, public API  
       • apis.js – module registration  
       • auto/ – injector  
       • jqLite.js – lightweight jQuery substitute  
       • ng/ – core services & directives (compile, $http, $q, $scope, $interpolate, etc.)  
       • ngAnimate, ngAria, ngCookies, ngLocale, ngMock, ngMessages, ngMessageFormat, ngParseExt, ngResource, ngRoute, ngSanitize, ngTouch – optional modules  
       • utilities (minErr, shallowCopy, routeToRegExp, stringify)  
   - test/          ← unit and E2E specs validating each core subcomponent  
   - docs/          ← documentation site generator, templates, assets  
   - i18n/          ← internationalization support, data extraction, locale files  
   - scripts/ & Gruntfile.js / gulpfile.js ← build, release, deployment, continuous integration helpers  
   - lib/, vendor/  ← third-party tools (promises-aplus adapter, SauceLabs scripts)  

3. Readme insights  
   - Emphasizes MV* pattern, dependency injection, two-way data binding, templating, modules, and testability.  
   - No runtime backend dependency—API calls happen via $http to external servers.  

4. How to diagram the system architecture  
   a. Main components:  
      1. Browser / Host Application  
      2. AngularJS Loader & Core  
           • Injector & Module Loader  
           • Compiler / Linker (template parsing & directive instantiation)  
           • $rootScope & Scope hierarchy (data binding engine)  
           • Core Services ($http, $q, $location, $timeout, etc.)  
           • jqLite DOM abstraction  
      3. Optional Modules (ngAnimate, ngRoute, ngResource, ngSanitize, ngTouch, etc.)  
      4. User-written Application Code (app modules, controllers, directives, templates)  
      5. External APIs / Backends (via $http / $resource)  
      6. Build & Test Pipeline  
           • Grunt/Gulp build tasks (concat, annotate, minify)  
           • Tests (unit → Karma, E2E → Protractor)  
           • Docs generator (docs/config → docs/app)  
   b. Relationships & interactions:  
      - On page load, the Loader reads angular.js → creates global angular object → invokes injector → modules register services, directives, filters.  
      - The Compiler traverses the DOM → matches directives → links templates to scopes → sets up watchers.  
      - Scopes digest loop synchronizes model ↔ view.  
      - Services like $http/$resource communicate asynchronously with External APIs.  
      - Optional modules plug into the core via the injector (e.g., ngAnimate provides animation hooks to the compile/link process).  
      - Build scripts take src/ → run lint/tests → produce concatenated/minified bundles → deploy via scripts/ to code.angularjs.org, etc.  
   c. Architectural patterns & principles:  
      - MV* / Declarative templates  
      - Dependency Injection (inversion of control)  
      - Modular architecture (core + optional modules)  
      - Promise-based async ($q)  
      - Layered design: Loader → Injector → Compiler → Runtime (scopes & services)  
   d. Key technologies & libraries:  
      - JavaScript ES5, jqLite (subset of jQuery)  
      - Grunt/Gulp for build  
      - Karma + Jasmine for unit tests  
      - Protractor for E2E tests  
      - Firebase functions for docs hosting  
      - Promises-A+ test adapter  

5. Tailoring the diagram to this library project  
   - Emphasize the plugin architecture: show how optional modules (ngAnimate, ngRoute, etc.) hook into core extension points.  
   - Show the build & release pipeline separately (linting, testing, bundling, publishing to cdn/code.angularjs.org).  
   - Highlight the absence of an internal database—external data flows through $http/$resource.  
   - Illustrate the docs site generator as a distinct subsystem that processes docs/config + content → static site under docs/app.  

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use clear, distinct shapes:  
       • Rectangles for runtime components (Loader, Injector, Compiler, Services)  
       • Cloud icons for External APIs / Backends  
       • Cylinders only if you need to represent persistent storage (none here)  
       • Parallel rectangles or “swim-lanes” to separate Build/Test/Docs pipelines from Runtime  
   - Color-code by layer:  
       • Core engine (blue)  
       • Optional modules (green)  
       • Application code (orange)  
       • External systems (gray)  
       • Build/Test/Docs (purple)  
   - Label all arrows with data or control flow:  
       • “module registration,” “template compilation,” “digest cycle,” “HTTP request/response,” “build artifact.”  
   - Show directional arrows:  
       • From Browser to Loader to Injector to Compiler  
       • Bidirectional between Scope and View (data binding)  
       • From Services to External APIs and back  

7. Key elements to capture  
   - Loader → Injector → Module registry  
   - Compiler & Directive instantiation  
   - Scope hierarchy & Watchers / Digest cycle  
   - Core Services and their extension by optional modules  
   - User application code consuming the framework  
   - Build/Test/Docs subsystems  

By breaking AngularJS into its core engine, optional modules, application-level code, external data sources, and build/test pipelines—and by using shapes, colors, and directional arrows—you’ll create an accurate, detailed system design diagram that reflects the full complexity of this framework project.
